events.title: Russia Parliamentary Election Winner
events.description:
Parliamentary elections are to be scheduled to be held in Russia in September 2026.

This market will resolve according to the political party that wins the greatest number of seats in the next Russian State Duma election.

If the results are not known definitively by September 30, 2027, 11:59 PM ET, this market will resolve to "Other".

In the event of a tie between multiple parties for the most seats won, this market will resolve in favor of the party that received a greater number of valid votes. In the event that results in a tie, this market will resolve in favor of the party whose listed abbreviation appears first in alphabetical order.

This market's resolution will be based solely on the number of seats won by the named party in the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation.

This market will resolve based on the results of this election as indicated by a consensus of credible reporting. If there is ambiguity, this market will resolve based solely on the official results reported by Russian government sources such as the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation.

Note: If a listed party contests the election as part of a jointly listed coalition with one or more parties not listed in this market, the market corresponding to the listed party will represent the coalition and will count all seats won by the coalition collectively. If two or more listed parties contest the election as a jointly listed coalition, with or without additional parties not listed in this market, the market corresponding to the party within that coalition that won the most seats in the previous election will represent the coalition and will count all seats won by the coalition collectively. If such a coalition dissolves, each market will again represent its respective party individually.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves based on the official seat count for the State Duma IX convocation as reported by the Central Election Commission (CEC). Resolution occurs following the election on September 20, 2026. The target condition is the party winning the greatest number of seats out of the 450 total deputies. If results remain unknown by September 30, 2027, the market resolves to 'Other'. As of July 28, 2026, the election has not occurred, and the resolution threshold (plurality of seats) hasn't been met.

## Source History & Current Reading

As of late July 2026, the CEC has registered 5 major parliamentary parties for the election, including United Russia, KPRF, LDPR, New People, and A Just Russia. Recent WCIOM polling (week of July 13-19, 2026) places United Russia's voting intention at 32.7%, with rival parties including KPRF (11.9%), New People (10.5%), LDPR (9.6%), and A Just Russia (5.4%). Historical data from 2021 confirms United Russia secured 324 initial seats (72% of 450) and 343 seats in 2016.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-25**: Reports indicate United Russia's electoral support dipped to approximately 32.7%-33% in mid-July FOM and VCIOM polling.
- **2026-07-24**: VCIOM analytical review for July 13-19 reports United Russia support at 32.7%, showing a 2.6 percentage point decline compared to the previous week.
- **2026-07-23**: Investigative reports suggest the Presidential Administration reduced United Russia's internal target to 45% of the vote.
- **2026-07-23**: CEC completes the registration of federal lists for all five parliamentary parties, formally starting the active campaign phase.
- **2026-06-24**: CEC adopts specialized voting and security procedures for elections in annexed/occupied territories and frontier regions.
- **2026-06-17**: Formal Presidential decree sets September 20, 2026, as the official election date, confirmed by CEC resolution.

## Key Factors

### 1. Structural and Incumbency Advantage _(raises)_

United Russia operates as the established ruling party with systemic access to administrative resources and significant dominance in 225 single-member districts. In previous cycles, this structure has converted vote shares in the 30-50% range into consistent absolute majorities (300+ seats). There are currently no organized opposition forces demonstrating the capacity to disrupt this systemic advantage in district-level contests.

### 2. Stable Polling Lead _(raises)_

Despite recent fluctuations and a modest downward trend, national polling shows United Russia consistently leading the nearest opposition parties by a margin of approximately 3:1. With UR polling at ~33% and individual rivals (KPRF, New People, LDPR) polling at 10-12%, the electoral landscape remains highly stable relative to the threshold required for a plurality victory.

### 3. Target Revision and Legitimacy Management _(uncertain)_

Reports regarding the Kremlin reducing ER's internal target to 45% of the vote suggest a proactive pivot to manage public perception and legitimacy rather than an indicator of electoral vulnerability. This adjustment reflects a preference for controlled, realistic margins rather than a reduction in overall systemic control.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

In every Duma election cycle under the current mixed electoral system (since 2016), United Russia has captured a comfortable plurality and absolute majority of the 450 seats. They held 343 seats (76%) in 2016 and 324 seats (72%) initially in 2021. No other party has come close to United Russia's seat total, with primary opposition parties historically hovering around 10-13% of total representation.

## Bottom Line

The primary uncertainty centers on the magnitude of United Russia's expected supermajority rather than the plurality outcome, as there is currently no evidence of a coalition or opposition party swing capable of closing the ~200+ seat gap required to overtake United Russia. The market outcome assumes the continued dominance of the ruling party, with the main dynamic being the Kremlin's targeted management of the party's final share of seats.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves based on the official winner of the Clacton parliamentary by-election, as declared by the Tendring District Council and recognized by the UK Parliament. The formal polling day is scheduled for Thursday, 13 August 2026. The resolution must be determined by June 30, 2027, 11:59 PM ET. As of July 28, 2026, the election date is set, and the official candidate list is finalized, with the result subject to the count on polling day.

## Source History & Current Reading

The vacancy for the Clacton constituency was formally created on July 8, 2026, when Nigel Farage was appointed Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead, a procedure used for resignation. The by-election writ was moved on July 9, 2026. The Tendring District Council published the Statement of Persons Nominated (SOPN) in mid-July 2026, confirming a record 34 candidates. Statutory deadlines for voter registration reached on July 28, 2026, with postal voting deadlines set for July 29, 2026, and proxy voting for August 5, 2026.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-28**: Voter registration deadline for the Clacton by-election expires.
- **2026-07-17**: Deadline for nominations passes; Statement of Persons Nominated confirms a record 34 candidates.
- **2026-07-13**: Official notice of election is issued by the Returning Officer.
- **2026-07-09**: House of Commons approves the moving of the writ for the Clacton by-election.
- **2026-07-08**: Nigel Farage formally leaves his seat via appointment as Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead.
- **2026-07-07**: Nigel Farage announces his resignation as MP for Clacton and his intent to stand in the resulting by-election.

## Key Factors

### 1. Structural Constituency Favourability _(raises)_

Clacton has distinct demographic characteristics, including an older population, approximately 73.0% Leave-voting in 2016, and low graduate density, which historically correlates with Reform UK's national support base. In the 2024 general election, Nigel Farage secured 46.2% of the vote with an 18.3 percentage point majority. This historical performance provides a strong local baseline that remains the primary indicator of electoral support, given the absence of direct by-election polling.

### 2. High Candidate Fragmentation _(raises)_

Tendring District Council has confirmed a record 34 candidates are standing in the by-election. This unusually large field likely spreads anti-Farage and anti-Reform sentiment across a wide array of minor party and independent candidates, such as Count Binface, The Reclaim Party, and others. In a first-past-the-post system, such extreme fragmentation typically prevents the consolidation of opposition voters around a main challenger, effectively lowering the bar for the incumbent to retain the seat.

### 3. National Reputational and Financial Scrutiny _(lowers)_

National polling (e.g., YouGov) indicates that 60% of GB adults believe Farage has not been honest regarding his finances, and 43% oppose the decision to hold the by-election. While there is no direct Clacton-specific polling, persistent negative national media coverage and public sentiment regarding the reasons for the by-election pose a risk of dampening turnout or alienating moderate voters who supported Reform in 2024 but are sensitive to these reputational issues.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Since 2010, the strategy of a sitting MP resigning through the Chiltern Hundreds or Manor of Northstead to trigger a by-election and immediately re-contest the same seat has been utilized multiple times in the UK, including cases like Douglas Carswell (Clacton, 2014) and Zac Goldsmith (Richmond Park, 2016). In this reference class, the resigning incumbent has consistently stood as a candidate and often succeeded in being re-elected, indicating that the move is a deliberate strategic choice rather than an anomaly in parliamentary practice.

## Bottom Line

The outcome is contingent on whether Nigel Farage’s established local support base holds against the dual pressures of national reputational scrutiny and the strategic risk of a 34-candidate field. The critical uncertainty is the lack of constituency-level polling, leaving the effect of negative national sentiment on local voters as an unquantified variable. The election will resolve whether the 'people versus the establishment' framing successfully engages the local electorate or whether the unusual number of candidates and financial controversy create a sufficient barrier to his re-election.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to the winner of the 2026 California gubernatorial election, scheduled for November 3, 2026, as confirmed by a consensus call from the Associated Press, Fox News, and NBC. If consensus is not reached by July 31, 2027, the market will resolve to 'Other' based on official certification. Currently, the election has not occurred, and the resolution threshold is pending. Xavier Becerra is a qualified candidate who advanced from the June 2, 2026 primary.

## Source History & Current Reading

As of July 28, 2026, polling indicates Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton. A Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) poll conducted June 29–July 6, 2026, of 1,578 adults shows Becerra at 61% and Hilton at 36%. An earlier Emerson College poll (May 27–28, 2026) showed Becerra at 28% in the primary, and an April 2026 RCP open-primary average placed Becerra at 6.0% before the field thinned and he emerged as the primary Democratic option.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-06**: PPIC statewide poll released, showing Xavier Becerra at 61% and Steve Hilton at 36%.
- **2026-06-14**: General election runoff field confirmed following the June 2 statewide primary, with Becerra and Hilton advancing.
- **2026-06-05**: AP reports Xavier Becerra advanced to the general election for California governor.
- **2026-06-02**: California top-two primary election held.
- **Spring 2026**: Kamala Harris announces she will not run for California governor, significantly reshaping the Democratic candidate field.

## Key Factors

### 1. Partisan Structural Advantage _(raises)_

California has a nearly 2-to-1 Democratic registration advantage over Republicans. In every California gubernatorial general election from 2010 through 2022, the Democratic nominee has won. Historical results show Democratic candidates consistently securing mid-50s to low-60s in percentage terms, while Republicans stay in the high-30s to low-40s. Overcoming this requires a structural shift of approximately 18–20 percentage points, a magnitude not observed in recent California history.

### 2. Candidate Campaign Positioning _(raises)_

Following the consolidation of the Democratic field after the June 2, 2026, primary, Xavier Becerra emerged as the leading Democratic figure. His campaign has gained visibility through his role as an honorary co-chair of the 'No on 39 – Block Trump’s Election Rigging' committee, which has raised over $2 million. Polling from July 2026 shows Becerra leading his Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, by a wide margin of 61% to 36%, reinforcing his path to holding the coalition required for victory.

### 3. Turnout and Base Consolidation _(uncertain)_

While statewide partisan alignment favors Democrats, general election turnout is volatile and historically lower in non-presidential cycles. Polling shows that Republican candidate Steve Hilton consolidated 59% of Republican voters in late May 2026. The outcome relies on whether Democratic turnout mirrors the 2018 high-salience cycle or the lower participation levels seen in midterm years, alongside the behavior of the roughly 20-30% of voters who were undecided or supported minor candidates during the primary phase.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Since 1998, Democrats have won the California governorship in 1998, 2010, 2014, 2018, and 2022. The only Republican victory in this timeframe occurred in 2006 (Arnold Schwarzenegger, 55.9%). Democratic winners typically clear 50% to 62% of the vote, and no Republican candidate has exceeded 41% since 2006.

## Bottom Line

The market outcome depends on whether Xavier Becerra can maintain his current double-digit polling lead (61% vs 36% in July 2026) through November 3, 2026. The primary uncertainty is not his position, but whether any late-stage political events or unforeseen shifts in electorate turnout could produce a historic deviation from the approximately 20-point structural Democratic advantage, which is required for an 'Other' or Republican-win outcome.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to the total number of unique individuals who officially hold the office of Prime Minister of the United Kingdom between the market start date of July 6, 2026, and December 31, 2027, at 11:59 PM ET. The primary resolution source is official information from the Government of the United Kingdom, supplemented by consensus of credible reporting. The individuals must be officially appointed by the Monarch to count; interim or caretaker roles do not count as separate unique individuals if the individual is not permanently appointed. Keir Starmer, who was serving as Prime Minister at market launch, counts as the first individual. Andy Burnham, appointed following Starmer, counts as the second. Currently, 2 unique individuals have held the office within this window.

## Source History & Current Reading

Keir Starmer held the office of Prime Minister at the start of the market on July 6, 2026. Following cumulative pressure from local election losses—where Labour lost 1,496 council seats—and internal party dissatisfaction, Starmer announced his intention to resign on June 22, 2026. He formally resigned as Prime Minister on July 20, 2026. Andy Burnham was subsequently invited by King Charles III to form a government and was officially appointed as Prime Minister on July 20, 2026, becoming the 59th individual to hold the office.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **July 20, 2026**: Keir Starmer formally resigns as Prime Minister; Andy Burnham is appointed to the office by the King.
- **June 22, 2026**: Keir Starmer announces his intention to resign and requests the Labour Party set a timetable for a leadership contest.
- **May 12, 2026**: Reuters reports Prime Minister Starmer struggling to save his job with internal pressure and calls for an exit timetable rising among MPs.
- **May 5, 2026**: Labour suffers significant losses in local elections, losing 1,496 councillors and control of 38 councils.

## Key Factors

### 1. Labour Party Leadership Stability _(uncertain)_

The UK Prime Minister holds their position by virtue of being the leader of the party holding the majority in the House of Commons (Labour won 403 of 650 seats in 2024). Stability is contingent on the leader's ability to maintain support from at least 81 Labour MPs (20% of the parliamentary party), which is the threshold required to trigger a leadership challenge. With Burnham now in office, his stability depends on navigating the same structural pressures that unseated Starmer, specifically economic performance and electoral volatility, such as the 25% national voting intention recently polled by Reform UK.

### 2. Constitutional and Parliamentary Mechanisms _(raises)_

Under the UK parliamentary system, there is no requirement for a general election when a governing party replaces its leader; the new leader effectively becomes the Prime Minister. Because Labour maintains its 403-seat majority, any future leadership removal (through resignation or a successful challenge by 81+ MPs) would immediately trigger the appointment of a new Prime Minister by the Monarch without recourse to the public. The timeline for such a transition can be rapid, as evidenced by the 2026 leadership contest processes handled by the NEC.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Between 1945 and 2026, there have been 16 Prime Ministers, 10 of whom first took office mid-term rather than immediately following a general election. The decade 2016–2026 saw extreme volatility, with 7 different Prime Ministers serving during this period, representing an average turnover of 0.7 Prime Ministers per year. Historical high-turnover periods include 1761–1768 (5 Prime Ministers between elections) and 1935–1945 (3 Prime Ministers between elections).

## Bottom Line

The market resolution count is currently 2, established by the tenures of Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham. Since only one of these, or a future third individual, needs to hold the office to satisfy the condition of 'two' unique Prime Ministers, the primary uncertainty is whether a third individual will be appointed by the Monarch before December 31, 2027. This depends entirely on the internal stability of the Labour government's leadership under Burnham and its resilience against a potential future leadership challenge or resignation.

events.title: Largest IPO by market cap in 2026?
events.description:
This market will resolve to the company that achieves the highest market capitalization in U.S. dollars based on the official closing price on its first trading day in 2026.

This market will resolve to a company that completes an Initial Public Offering (IPO) between January 1 and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET.

Market capitalization is defined as the total number of outstanding shares multiplied by the closing share price on the first trading day.

If two or more companies have exactly equal highest closing market capitalizations, this market will resolve to the company whose listed name comes first alphabetically.

Resolution will be based on the primary exchange’s official listing page. In the event that the relevant figure is not displayed, another reliable source will be used.

In case the respective company's primary exchange’s official listing page does not report in U.S. dollars, it will be converted to U.S. dollars using the U.S. Federal Reserve Board’s H.10 foreign exchange reference rate for the relevant currency pair on the company’s first trading day (https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h10/). If no such rate is available for the relevant trading day, the most recent previously published rate will be used. If the relevant currency is not listed, another credible exchange rate source will be used.

A listed company may resolve to "No" as soon as it becomes unable to complete an IPO, including due to acquisition, merger, or absorption by an entity that is already publicly traded.

In the event of an interruption in the course of the normal trading session on the respective companies’ first day of trading (e.g., a circuit breaker or half-day), the market will resolve according to the official closing price of the abbreviated session. If no such official closing price is published, the market will resolve according to the next trading day on which an official closing price is published, treating that as the first day of trading for purposes of this market.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to the company that completes an IPO between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2026, that achieves the highest market capitalization in U.S. dollars based on the official closing price on its first trading day. Market capitalization is calculated as total outstanding shares multiplied by the closing share price. The current benchmark is SpaceX (ticker: SPCX), which attained a first-day closing market cap of approximately $2.1 trillion on June 12, 2026. To resolve to a different company, a subsequent 2026 IPO must exceed this $2.1 trillion threshold. Resolution sources include the primary exchange's official listing or the Federal Reserve H.10 reference rate for currency conversions.

## Source History & Current Reading

SpaceX (ticker: SPCX) completed its IPO on June 12, 2026, with an offering price of $135.00 and roughly 638,888,888 shares sold, closing at approximately $161, resulting in a market cap of over $2 trillion. Other notable 2026 IPOs include Cerebras Systems (May 14, 2026, ~$5.6 billion market cap) and Czechoslovak Group (Jan 23, 2026, ~$39 billion market cap). Renaissance Capital reports ~$251 billion in US equity issuance through H1 2026, though this total is heavily skewed by the SpaceX mega-listing.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **July 28, 2026**: Analysis of mid-year 2026 figures indicates high IPO proceeds but a concentration of record valuation in the SpaceX event rather than a broad market boom.
- **June 15, 2026**: SpaceX formally files an 8-K confirming the completion of the IPO and the restructuring of its capital formation in Texas.
- **June 12, 2026**: SpaceX listing on Nasdaq/Nasdaq Texas establishes the initial benchmark of ~$2.1 trillion market cap.

## Key Factors

### 1. SpaceX Benchmark _(lowers)_

The $2.1 trillion threshold is an extreme statistical outlier. Historically, even the most successful mega-cap IPOs (e.g., Rivian at ~$66B, Arm at ~$54.5B) have landed in the $10 billion to $70 billion range. Achieving a valuation 30 times higher than typical historical ceilings makes the probability of any other company surpassing this mark in 2026 negligible under standard market conditions.

### 2. IPO Pipeline Depth _(lowers)_

Public pipeline trackers through late July 2026 show no entities approaching a $1 trillion+ valuation. Most major unicorn candidates (e.g., Stripe, Databricks) lack confirmed IPO dates, have de-prioritized listings, or possess valuations far below the required $2 trillion mark. The H2 2026 pipeline is projected to be dominated by mid-cap incumbents rather than high-valuation tech mega-unicorns.

### 3. Unicorn Valuation Gap _(lowers)_

Top remaining unicorns like OpenAI (~$852 billion) and Anthropic (~$965 billion) would require an immediate 2.2x to 2.5x multiple expansion upon listing relative to their current private valuations to breach the SpaceX threshold. Such an uplift on a first-day public debut is historically unprecedented for companies of that maturity.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Historical US IPOs from 2021-2025 demonstrate that first-day market caps almost exclusively fall in the $10B to $70B bracket. SpaceX's ~$2.1T debut is a massive anomaly, representing a valuation an order of magnitude larger than any relevant historical high-water mark.

## Bottom Line

The outcome is binary: any company listing in H2 2026 must eclipse the $2.1 trillion barrier. This would require an extreme and currently unobserved market deviation where a private unicorn such as OpenAI or Anthropic is re-valued by the public market at twice its current private mark. Absent a radical, systemic reassessment of AI-company valuations, the current SpaceX figure is expected to remain the highest of the year.

As of July 26, 2026, the official House Clerk roster lists 218 Republicans, 212 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 4 vacancies. National generic ballot polls published in July 2026 consistently show a Democratic lead of 5-7 percentage points, including Nate Silver's D+6.1, Decision Desk HQ's D+6, and Pew's D+6. - **2026-07-27**: The Orange County Register reports that the number of competitive House districts has fallen to 37, with Democrats holding a 10-point advantage in voter enthusiasm.
- **2026-07-24**: POLITICO polls indicate 46% of Americans believe gas prices influence their vote, with both parties planning messaging campaigns focused on affordability.

### 1. Current House Composition and Vulnerability _(lowers)_

With the 119th Congress holding 218 Republicans and 212 Democrats, Republicans hold a bare-majority 218-seat threshold. Approximately 37 districts are classified by major organizations such as the Cook Political Report as competitive. Because Republicans currently hold a narrow 2-seat margin above the 218 threshold, any net loss of 6 or more seats would likely shift the majority. Analysis of competitive districts confirms that 16 of the top 20 most competitive seats are currently held by Republicans, creating a significant structural vulnerability for the party.

### 2. Generic Congressional Ballot Polling _(lowers)_

National generic ballot polling consistently places Democrats ahead by 5 to 7 percentage points as of late July 2026. Models such as Decision Desk HQ and the Silver Bulletin indicate this stable lead has persisted since April 2026. Historical context shows this level of generic ballot lead is comparable to prior strong Democratic midterm environments, and uniform-swing simulations suggest a D+6 environment would potentially flip enough Republican-held seats to produce a Democratic majority.

### 3. Presidential Approval Ratings _(lowers)_

Trump's approval rating as of July 2026 is trapped in the 34% to 40% range, with disapproval ratings near 60% in most major surveys including Gallup and Pew. Historical analysis confirms a strong linear correlation between presidential job approval and seat loss; presidents with job approval below 50% historically suffer an average loss of 37 House seats. The high intensity of disapproval (nearly half of voters strongly disapprove) and the tendency for voters to frame midterm elections as referendums against unpopular presidents weigh heavily on Republican incumbents.

### 4. Fundraising and Resource Deployment _(uncertain)_

As of June 2026, the NRCC holds a central committee-level cash advantage of approximately $13.7 million over the DCCC (NRCC $92.7 million vs. DCCC $79 million). Furthermore, high-profile Democratic candidates are outraising numerous GOP incumbents in competitive districts, creating a two-track battlefield where Republicans have national committee-level advantages while Democrats show local fundraising strength.

### 5. Historical Midterm Patterns _(lowers)_

Since 1946, the president's party has lost House seats in 18 out of 20 midterm elections (90%). In the last 50 years, the presidential party lost House seats in 11 of 13 cycles. The current baseline shows the president's party is historically prone to significant reversals, often ranging from 9 to 41 seats in recent cycles. Given the Republicans' current narrow 2-seat margin, historical volatility trends overwhelmingly point to a high risk of losing the majority, as 5+ seats change hands in nearly all modern midterm cycles.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Since 1946, the president's party has lost House seats in 18 out of 20 midterm elections (90%). In recent cycles, losses have ranged from 9 seats (2022) to 41 seats (2018). With a current majority of only 2 seats, the current GOP structure deviates only slightly from the historical baseline of high vulnerability for the party holding the presidency.

## Bottom Line

The fundamental tension lies between the structural, historical headwinds facing the president's party—90% of midterms result in seat losses—and the narrow 2-seat Republican margin on the table. events.title: How many Fed rate cuts in 2026?
events.description:
This market will resolve according to the exact amount of cuts of 25 basis points in 2026 by the Fed (including any cuts made during the December meeting).

Emergency rate cuts outside of scheduled FOMC meetings will also count toward the total number of cuts in 2026. This market will remain open until December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET, to account for any such emergency actions.

For example, if the Fed cuts rates by 50 bps after a meeting, it would be considered 2 cuts (of 25 bps each).

This market will resolve early to "No" if the specified number of cuts becomes impossible — i.e., if more cuts have already occurred than the strike in question.

Note that cuts between 1–24 bps (inclusive) will also be considered 1 rate cut.

The resolution source for this market will be FOMC statements after meetings scheduled in 2026 according to the official calendar: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm. ## Resolution Mechanics

This market resolves to 'Yes' if the total number of 25 basis point rate cuts implemented by the Federal Reserve in 2026 is exactly 0. The resolution source is official FOMC statements and the official Federal Reserve target federal funds rate page (https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm). As of July 28, 2026, the count of 25-basis-point rate cuts remains 0. The threshold for the 'Yes' outcome is 0 cuts, while any positive number of 25-bp cuts results in 'No'.

## Source History & Current Reading

The current target federal funds rate is 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, a range established by a cut on December 10, 2025. From January 1, 2026, through July 28, 2026, the FOMC has held this rate constant at all scheduled meetings (April 28–29 and June 16–17). No emergency rate cuts have occurred in 2026.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-13**: Governor Christopher Waller signals in a speech that he requires several months of lower core inflation readings to reconsider the current policy rate, noting core PCE rose from 3.0% in December 2025 to 3.4% in May 2026.
- **2026-06-17**: FOMC meeting concludes; the committee votes to maintain the target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. The released Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) shows a median 2026 federal funds rate projection of 3.8%.
- **2026-06-16–17**: FOMC minutes show members unanimously commit to a price stability mandate, emphasizing a cautious path of gradual adjustments.
- **2026-04-29**: FOMC meeting minutes record almost all members support no change in the target range, with the Desk survey showing market participants expect little change in the target range for 2026.

## Key Factors

### 1. Inflationary Environment _(raises)_

The Fed's target measure for inflation, PCE, remains above the 2% objective. Headline PCE was 4.1% and core PCE 3.4% as of May 2026, representing an increase from late 2025 levels. While June 2026 CPI data showed headline cooling to 3.5% and core to 2.6%, Fed officials, including Governor Waller, have stated that a few months of data are insufficient to trigger a policy pivot, favoring a 'hold' or 'hike' bias.

### 2. FOMC Policy Projections and Stance _(raises)_

The June 2026 Summary of Economic Projections indicates a median 2026 policy rate of 3.8%, which is higher than the range established in the previous March projection. Furthermore, internal votes have remained unanimous for unchanged rates throughout 2026. Forward guidance emphasizes price stability over early easing, limiting the likelihood of cuts.

### 3. Labor Market Conditions _(raises)_

FOMC participants and associated commentary place the unemployment rate near a 4% equilibrium level. Because employment is currently assessed consistent with stable growth rather than recessionary weakness, there is limited pressure on the Fed to deploy rate cuts as a counter-cyclical stimulus measure in late 2026.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Since the beginning of 2026, the FOMC has held the target federal funds rate unchanged at all held meetings. Market-implied pricing from the CME FedWatch tool for the 2026 July, September, October, and December meetings consistently assigns the highest probability weight to either 'hold' or 'hike' outcomes across all snapshots observed through July 2026.

## Bottom Line

The trajectory of the 'no rate cuts' outcome depends heavily on whether economic data forces a shift from the current 'higher for longer' posture. Key developments that would deviate from this path include severe, sustained deterioration in labor market data (unemployment spiking well above 4%) or unexpected, sharp sustained disinflation that conflicts with the committee's current inflation risk assessment. Conversely, if inflation remains stubbornly above 2% or increases, the committee’s bias is toward maintaining or potentially increasing the policy rate, which would secure the 'Yes' outcome.

## Source History & Current Reading

As of July 28, 2026: Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in a US-Israeli strike on March 8, 2026. The 88-member Assembly of Experts formally appointed Mojtaba Khamenei as Supreme Leader on March 8, 2026. IRGC and affiliated institutions control approximately 50 percent of Iran's oil wealth. Mojtaba Khamenei has had zero public appearances since March 2026, communicating exclusively through written messages. The SNSC, which includes the presidency, judiciary, IRGC, and intelligence services, is the primary locus of daily governing control.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-21**: President Masoud Pezeshkian states Iran's policies continue under Supreme Leader guidance and claims 'greater access' to Mojtaba Khamenei.
- **2026-07-06**: Reports characterize Mojtaba as Iran's new supreme leader but note he remains unseen and communicates through written directives.
- **2026-06-14**: Reporting confirms Mojtaba Khamenei approved diplomatic negotiations with the US, with President Pezeshkian and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf playing central roles.
- **2026-03-08**: Ayatollah Ali Khamenei is killed in a strike on Tehran; the Assembly of Experts holds an extraordinary session and appoints Mojtaba Khamenei as the third leader of the Islamic Republic.
- **2026-03-01**: A three-person interim leadership council comprising Pezeshkian, Mohseni-Ejei, and Alireza Arafi is formed under Article 111 following the death of Ali Khamenei.

### 1. IRGC Institutional Dominance _(lowers)_

The IRGC has consolidated control over approximately 50 percent of state-adjacent economic assets and dominates the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), which serves as the primary executive board after the 12-day war. Because current reporting indicates that Mojtaba Khamenei's role is largely legitimizing decisions forged by the IRGC and SNSC rather than exercising independent control over armed forces or core executive decisions, this structural reality limits the likelihood of him being recognized as the primary de facto ruler.

### 2. Mojtaba Khamenei's Health and Public Absence _(lowers)_

Since his appointment on March 8, 2026, Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared in public and has allegedly suffered injuries, communicating only via written statements. This persistent absence undermines his capability to exercise the tangible, daily executive functions (such as leading meetings, commanding forces, or issuing binding verbal directives) required for the de facto head-of-state threshold.

### 3. Formal Appointment and Constitutional Mandate _(raises)_

The Assembly of Experts, comprised of 88 vetted clerics, acted under Article 108 on March 8, 2026, to formally appoint Mojtaba Khamenei as Supreme Leader. While his rule is reported as symbolic, this formal status provides him with the legal legitimacy required for the position. The Assembly's decisive vote against a protracted leadership vacuum provides the base standing that necessitates the market to track his continued status against actual power dynamics.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

The Islamic Republic has seen only one prior comparable transition, the 1989 succession from Khomeini to Ali Khamenei. In that instance, the transition followed a pre-planned consolidation. The current structure, characterized by military-security capture (IRGC controlling approximately 50 percent of oil wealth and key security bodies), aligns with other late-stage revolutionary regimes where the formal religious head remains as a symbolic figurehead while security institutions exert actual governing power. Historically, the position is designed for life; changes to the individual holding the title are rare and event-driven (total 2 successions in ~47 years).

## Bottom Line

The primary uncertainty is whether the existing 'symbolic-head plus security-collective' model persists or whether internal power struggles within the IRGC or the potential for a formal move toward constitutional change (e.g., merging the presidency and supreme leader positions) will occur by end of 2026. # Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to 'Yes' if Paramount closes its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery's studios and streaming businesses by June 30, 2027, 11:59 PM ET. Non-finalized arrangements and transactions limited to linear television, news, or non-studio/streaming assets do not qualify. Resolution is based on consensus reporting. The current status is a formal operational standstill: on July 24, 2026, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery agreed to a delay in closing until at least June 1, 2027, or until a ruling on the merits is reached in the antitrust trial. The market resolves to 'None by June 30 2027' if no closing occurs within the specified period.

## Source History & Current Reading

On July 24, 2026, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery agreed to suspend closing the transaction until June 1, 2027, or a merit-based court ruling in the antitrust state attorneys general lawsuit. This followed a July 20, 2026, temporary restraining order by a California federal court. Previously, the US DOJ cleared the deal on June 12, 2026, and the European Commission granted conditional clearance on July 22, 2026. The deal remains valued at approximately $111 billion, with ticking fees of $7 million per day applicable after September 30, 2026, and a $7 billion potential regulatory termination fee.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-28**: BBC report confirms the Paramount-WBD merger is paused amid legal challenges, with a potential standstill until June 1, 2027.
- **2026-07-24**: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery agree to delay closing until June 1, 2027, or a merits ruling, following a July 20 TRO.
- **2026-07-22**: European Commission provides conditional clearance for the Paramount-WBD deal, contingent on Paramount exiting its United International Pictures joint venture.
- **2026-07-20**: A federal court in California issues a TRO against the merger, identifying serious questions regarding market concentration in theatrical distribution.
- **2026-06-12**: The US DOJ closes an 8-month investigation into the transaction with no objection, finding no likely harm to competition in streaming or theatrical distribution.
- **2026-04-23**: WBD stockholders overwhelmingly approve the merger agreement.

## Key Factors

### 1. Antitrust Litigation and Structural Presumptions _(lowers)_

The 12-state attorneys general lawsuit is the most significant obstacle. The Clayton Act challenge focuses on theatrical distribution market share, specifically the combined entity's 27% stake in wide-release distribution and control of over 30% of anticipated blockbusters. The federal court's issuance of a temporary restraining order (TRO) cited 'serious questions' and a structural presumption of illegality. Because the preliminary injunction hearing was canceled in favor of a direct trial (targeted for April 2027), the outcome now depends entirely on overcoming this structural barrier in court. The June 1, 2027, standstill acts as a massive time-constraint, as any unfavorable trial ruling arriving just prior to or during June 2027 could render the deal dead before the contractually allowed June 30, 2027, resolution deadline.

### 2. Contractual Financial Pressure (Ticking and Termination Fees) _(lowers)_

While Paramount has secured committed equity ($47 billion) and debt ($49 billion) financing, the merger's financial viability is under increasing stress from the delayed timeline. If the deal does not close by September 30, 2026, Paramount incurs a 'ticking fee' of approximately $7 million per day, totaling about $650 million per quarter, and potentially up to $1.7 billion by June 2027. Additionally, if the deal fails due to a regulatory blockage, Paramount faces a $7 billion termination fee. The accumulation of these costs, combined with the extreme leverage of the new entity (~$79 billion estimated net debt), creates a high-stakes scenario where the board may be forced to renegotiate or abandon the deal if the judicial path remains uncertain into mid-2027.

### 3. Regulatory Divergence (International and US) _(uncertain)_

The regulatory landscape is split. The US DOJ formally cleared the deal, stating it would not harm competition in streaming or theatrical distribution, which provides a strong legal argument for Paramount at trial. However, the UK's Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy, has signaled intent to intervene on grounds of media plurality and on-demand programming control, with potential further legislation in the pipeline. Although European regulators cleared the deal (conditional on divesting United International Pictures), the ongoing, multifaceted regulatory reviews increase the operational complexity of closing by the June 2027 deadline, adding a layer of international risk to the primary US litigation hurdles.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

The merger involves the entirety of WBD's Studios and Streaming segments, representing roughly 132 million subscribers and approximately $23.5 billion in annual revenue as of 2025. Acquisitions of this specific 'Studio + Streaming' scope (the 'Retained Business' in the Netflix-model carve-out) are high-value, high-scrutiny events. Historically, media mergers of this magnitude ($110B+ enterprise value) that reach the state-AG litigation stage and trigger federal court TROs face extremely high bars for completion; they are not routine business combinations but transformational, high-antitrust-risk transactions.

## Bottom Line

The primary tension is between the contractual standstill (ending no later than June 1, 2027) and the June 30, 2027, market resolution date. The deal is structurally and contractually blocked until effectively June 2027. Success depends on victory in the state antitrust trial—scheduled for April 2027—and the subsequent rapid implementation of the deal before the end of the second quarter of 2027. The binary risk revolves around whether the trial concludes in Paramount's favor with enough lead time to finalize the merger. Any finding of liability or extended appellate process would likely preclude a closing by the resolution date.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to 'Yes' if the upper bound of the target federal funds rate is increased at any point between January 1, 2026, and the conclusion of the December 2026 FOMC meeting (scheduled for December 8-9, 2026). The Federal Reserve tracks the target range upper bound; as of the most recent decision effective June 18, 2026, the upper bound stands at 3.75% (within a 3.50% to 3.75% range). The metric has remained unchanged at 3.75% throughout all FOMC meetings in 2026 to date. The primary resolution source is the official Federal Reserve website (federalreserve.gov), with consensus of credible reporting as a secondary source. The threshold for 'Yes' is any single increase of the upper bound above the 3.75% level confirmed at any remaining 2026 meeting.

## Source History & Current Reading

As of the last recorded update on July 8, 2026, the FOMC has maintained the federal funds target range at 3.50%–3.75% for all 2026 meetings to date. Specifically, the directive effective January 29, 2026, maintained the range of 3.50%–3.75%, which was subsequently reaffirmed in meetings effective April 30, 2026, and June 18, 2026. The latest meeting minutes, last updated July 8, 2026, confirm no changes were made to the upper bound during the year. Board votes on administered rates (interest on reserve balances at 3.65% and the primary credit rate at 3.75%) have also remained constant throughout these periods.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-14**: June 2026 CPI report released; Headline CPI 3.5% YoY, Core CPI 2.6% YoY.
- **2026-07-13**: Governor Christopher Waller signals the Fed will consider tightening if core inflation doesn't cool, while keeping rates steady if progress continues.
- **2026-07-08**: FOMC June minutes updated, indicating split views on year-end trajectory with 9 of 18 policymakers projecting higher rates.
- **2026-07-02**: June jobs report shows +57,000 nonfarm payrolls and 4.2% unemployment rate.
- **2026-06-17**: FOMC concludes meeting; keeps target range at 3.50%–3.75% and removes easing bias.

## Key Factors

### 1. Fed Policy Projections and Dot Plot _(raises)_

The June 2026 Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) showed a median end-2026 policy rate of 3.8%, which is above the current 3.75% upper bound. Notably, 9 of 18 FOMC participants indicated they expected rates to be higher by year-end, signaling that a non-trivial portion of the Committee sees the possibility of policy firming if inflation data does not align with the 2% target. This provides a clear mechanism for a potential hike if incoming economic data creates significant upside surprises in inflation metrics.

### 2. Inflationary Data Trends _(raises)_

Inflation data entering mid-2026 has been mixed, with headline CPI dropping to 3.5% in June due to energy price declines, while PCE measures—the Fed's preferred metric—have remained elevated around 3.8%–4.1%. Persistent concern regarding core inflation staying above the 2% target remains a primary driver for policymakers. While June showed cooling in certain metrics, sustained inflation, particularly attributed to tariff increases and Middle East conflict-driven input costs, continues to create pressure that could warrant defensive policy action.

### 3. Labor Market and Economic Cooling _(lowers)_

Recent labor data reflects an evolving domestic economy, with nonfarm payrolls adding only 57,000 jobs in June and unemployment hovering near 4.2%–4.3%. While these figures suggest the economy is not overheating in a way that typically forces an immediate, aggressive hike, the FOMC characterized the labor market as 'balanced' rather than 'slack.' If the labor market were to deteriorate significantly, the impetus for a rate hike would diminish, as the Fed would prioritize avoiding overtightening.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

There are four remaining scheduled FOMC meetings in 2026 (July, September, October, and December) where a departure from the current 3.50%–3.75% target range could be decided. Historically, the Fed maintains rates unless exogenous shocks or significant data deviations occur; however, the Committee showed increased hawkishness in June by removing their 'easing bias,' broadening the set of outcomes to include potential hikes, which had not been the focus in the first half of the year.

## Bottom Line

The fundamental uncertainty for this market resolution rests on whether incoming CPI and PCE data for Q3 and Q4 2026 will convince the FOMC that current policy is insufficiently restrictive to reach the 2% inflation target. The market is currently balanced between a 'hold' or 'cut' path and a 'hike' path, with the FOMC's own SEP median suggesting a potential for a 3.8% peak. A 'Yes' resolution would require a change in data interpretation from the participants currently favoring or on the fence about a hike, specifically triggered by either a re-acceleration in core inflation or signs that the labor market can withstand higher borrowing costs without a disruptive contraction.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to Yes if the US House of Representatives, by simple majority vote, approves or passes one or more articles of impeachment between March 19, 2026 and January 20, 2029 at 12:00 PM ET. The current threshold is 218 votes. As of July 28, 2026, no such vote has passed the House floor, and H.Res. 1155, introduced on April 6, 2026, remains in the Judiciary Committee, meaning the market is currently at No.

## Source History & Current Reading

Legislative data from Congress.gov records the latest impeachment action as H.Res. 537, which occurred on June 24, 2025. The current 119th Congress has a Democratic majority estimated between 219 and 229 seats. H.Res. 1155, introduced April 6, 2026, by Rep. John Larson, is the only active impeachment resolution involving Donald Trump since March 2026.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-23**: House passed war-powers resolution by 214-208; Senate blocked companion bill.
- **2026-07-22**: House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan sent a criminal referral to the DOJ regarding former special counsel Jack Smith.
- **2026-07-14**: Reports emerged that Jack Smith's team reviewed text messages from 44 members of Congress.
- **2026-07-13**: President Trump notified Congress of resumed Iran hostilities.
- **2026-06-20**: Reports noted multiple House attempts to invoke war-powers authority over Iran.
- **2026-06-03**: House passed war-powers resolution on Iran by 215-208.
- **2026-04-06**: H.Res. 1155 formally introduced in House by Rep. John B. Larson.

## Key Factors

### 1. Democratic Majority Cohesion _(uncertain)_

The House majority currently sits at approximately 219-229 seats. Given that simple majority approval requires 218 votes, Democrats have an extremely thin margin. This necessitates nearly perfect caucus discipline for an impeachment vote to pass without meaningful GOP support, which is historically unlikely given high partisan polarization documented in 2026 generic ballot data. If the caucus size trends toward the lower bound of 219 seats, the margin for error is near zero.

### 2. Legislative Procedural Tools _(raises)_

House procedures allow for the Rules Committee to expedite impeachment articles directly to the floor, bypassing lengthy committee hearings if the majority leadership so desires, as demonstrated in the 2021 impeachment of President Trump. This procedural flexibility means that should the House leadership choose to prioritize impeachment, they can navigate floor consideration rapidly, meaning the primary barrier is leadership will rather than procedural or parliamentary complexity.

### 3. Political Catalyst Frequency _(raises)_

There is a consistent history of impeachment activity regarding President Trump, with three distinct impeachment episodes occurring between 2019 and 2025. Frequent legislative skirmishes, such as the ongoing war-powers disputes with Iran occurring as late as July 2026, suggest that the conditions for potential conflict between the House and the executive branch remain active and may produce future catalysts for impeachment proceedings.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Since 1974, there have been 10 presidential terms or partial terms. Two presidents (Clinton and Trump) have been impeached by the US House a total of four times (1998, 2019, 2021, 2025). The base rate for presidential impeachment by the House is approximately 0.4 episodes per presidency, though this figure is heavily skewed by the three impeachments of Donald Trump in recent years, which establishes a high-frequency outlier pattern compared to the 0-per-term baseline seen for other modern presidents.

## Bottom Line

The outcome hinges on whether the Democratic majority can maintain the 218-vote threshold necessary for an impeachment resolution in the face of narrow seat margins and partisan polarization. Potential catalysts include ongoing legislative conflict over war powers or new developments from committee referrals, but the lack of a House floor vote on H.Res. 1155 means the market threshold has not been met as of July 28, 2026.

events.title: Iran charges Hormuz fees by...?
events.description:
This market resolves to “Yes” if the Iranian government officially announces and begins collecting fees, tolls, charges, tariffs, or similar payments from commercial vessels which are mandatory for passage through or access to the Strait of Hormuz between market creation and the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market resolves to “No.”

A qualifying fee must be an announced policy which applies generally to all commercial vessels, or a defined subcategory of commercial vessels (e.g., vessels flagged to the US and its allies). Isolated demanded charges will not qualify.

A fee is mandatory if, in practice, affected commercial vessels cannot transit or access the Strait of Hormuz without paying it, regardless of whether Iran characterizes the payment as voluntary or a fee for services. Fees described as tolls, maritime fees, service charges, environmental fees, security fees, insurance charges, etc. will qualify provided they are recognized as mandatory for passage through or access to the Strait of Hormuz by a consensus of credible reporting (e.g., a mandatory insurance fee charged by the Iranian Persian Gulf Strait Authority would qualify).

Both of the following are required to occur prior to the specified date, 11:59 PM ET to satisfy this market’s resolution criteria:
1) An official announcement from the Iranian government that such a fee is being, or will be, implemented.
2) A consensus of credible reporting that collection of the fee has begun.

Fees charged by Oman, the United Arab Emirates, shipping insurers, private companies, or other non-Iranian entities do not qualify unless charged jointly with Iran, or if Iran directly receives the fee or controls the charging entity. Normal port fees, customs duties, sanctions-related costs, or shipping surcharges do not alone qualify. 

The resolution sources will be official announcements from the government of Iran and consensus of credible reporting.

Fees described as tolls, maritime fees, service charges, environmental fees, security fees, insurance charges, etc. will qualify provided they are recognized as mandatory for passage through or access to the Strait of Hormuz by a consensus of credible reporting (e.g., a mandatory insurance fee charged by the Iranian Persian Gulf Strait Authority would qualify).

Both of the following are required to occur prior to the specified date, 11:59 PM ET to satisfy this market’s resolution criteria:
1) An official announcement from the Iranian government that such a fee is being, or will be, implemented.
2) A consensus of credible reporting that collection of the fee has begun.

Fees charged by Oman, the United Arab Emirates, shipping insurers, private companies, or other non-Iranian entities do not qualify unless charged jointly with Iran, or if Iran directly receives the fee or controls the charging entity. Normal port fees, customs duties, sanctions-related costs, or shipping surcharges do not alone qualify. 

The resolution sources will be official announcements from the government of Iran and consensus of credible reporting.

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to 'Yes' if two conditions are met prior to 11:59 PM ET on the resolution date: 1) The Iranian government officially announces the implementation of fees, tolls, or charges (including service/environmental labels) mandatory for commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz, and 2) A consensus of credible reporting confirms the collection of these fees has begun. Current status as of July 28, 2026: Iran and the U.S. signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on June 19, 2026, which established a 60-day 'charge-free' transit period ending approximately August 18, 2026. The market for Aug 31 is highly sensitive to whether Iran formally re-imposes these charges immediately following the expiration of this waiver.

## Source History & Current Reading

On May 18, 2026, Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) established the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) to manage transit and collect fees (often cited at USD $1.5–2 million per vessel). Following a period of ad-hoc collection or demands, a June 19, 2026 MoU with the U.S. implemented a 60-day suspension of 'security, safety, environmental services, and related insurance' fees. As of July 28, 2026, recent reports from Fars News and other sources indicate Iran intends to resume these collections post-waiver, framing them as 'service fees' under a new legal-administrative framework.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-28**: Reports surface that Iran has begun plans to resume collection of 'service fees' (USD 1.5–2 million per ship) after the 60-day truce expires.
- **2026-07-20**: IRNA reports that the Iranian government is finalizing 'environmental compensation fees' for transit to be submitted to parliament.
- **2026-07-06**: Reports indicate Iran and Oman are negotiating a pay model for the Strait, with Iran demanding mandatory service fees.
- **2026-06-19**: SNSC and PGSA announce a formal 60-day waiver of all transit fees for vessels under an MoU with the United States.
- **2026-06-16**: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei frames future charges as 'maritime service fees' rather than transit tolls.
- **2026-05-18**: Iran officially launches the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) with a mandate to collect passage fees.

The current grace period, which effectively suspended 'security, safety, environmental, and insurance' fees, lasts for 60 days from its announcement on June 19, 2026, putting the tentative cutoff around August 18, 2026. The resolution of the August 31 market hinges entirely on whether Iran formalizes and initiates the collection of these fees immediately following this window. Recent statements from Iranian officials, including negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have consistently described the waiver as a temporary suspension rather than a permanent abandonment of the fee regime.

### 2. Legal Re-framing of Fees _(raises)_

Iran is actively maneuvering to bypass UNCLOS objections by re-labeling 'transit tolls' as 'maritime service,' 'navigation coordination,' or 'environmental protection' fees. By establishing the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) and drafting regulatory codes under Article 26(2) of UNCLOS (which theoretically allows limited charges for specific services), Iran provides itself a domestic legal basis to resume collection while dismissing the international consensus that any mandatory passage fee is illegal.

### 3. International Legal and Diplomatic Opposition _(lowers)_

The IMO, U.S. officials (including Secretary of State Marco Rubio), and numerous international maritime legal experts maintain that the Strait of Hormuz is an international waterway where transit passage cannot be impeded or taxed. If Iran imposes these fees, the international community's denial of their validity could complicate the 'consensus' requirement for market resolution.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves based on official results published by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) at https://dadosabertos.tse.jus.br/. The winner is the candidate who obtains an absolute majority of valid votes in the first round (October 4, 2026) or a simple majority in the second round (October 25, 2026). The current phase is administrative; official candidate registration is required by August 15, 2026. As of July 28, 2026, the election has not occurred, and no result is available; the market must resolve by June 30, 2027.

## Source History & Current Reading

The primary resolution source is the TSE official repository. The dataset 'Candidatos - 2026' was generated on July 22, 2026, and is updated daily. All historical election data (1998-2022) are archived in the TSE 'Resultados' database. Current status as of July 28, 2026: No official presidential candidates are registered in the TSE system, pending the August 15, 2026, filing deadline.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-27**: BTG/Nexus poll shows Lula with 47% vs Flávio Bolsonaro 43% in a second-round hypothetical matchup.
- **2026-07-24**: Datafolha survey reports Lula leads second round 48% to 43% vs Flávio Bolsonaro.
- **2026-07-22**: TSE open-data repository 'Candidatos - 2026' becomes publicly live with daily updates.
- **2026-07-20**: PDT party grants unanimous endorsement to Lula's reelection bid.
- **2025-10-24**: Lula publicly declares intent to run for his fourth term.

## Key Factors

### 1. Polling Aggregates for Second Round _(uncertain)_

As of late July 2026, polling indicates a persistent but narrowing lead for Lula. Datafolha (July 24, 2026) puts Lula at 48% vs. Flávio Bolsonaro at 43%, while BTG/Nexus (July 27, 2026) reflects similar figures (47% vs. 43%). These results place the matchup within or near the margin of error (±2 pp), indicating significant polarization and electoral competitiveness rather than an overwhelming incumbent advantage. The first-round polling shows Lula leading with 40-42% against the opposition's combined fragmented support.

### 2. Economic Indicators and Approval _(uncertain)_

Brazil reported record-low unemployment of 5.6% in 2025/2026 and moderate 2025 GDP growth of 2.3% with inflation within target (4.26% in 2025). Despite these figures, presidential job approval remains starkly split: Datafolha reports 49% approve vs. 48% disapprove, while Gerp reports 43% approve vs. 50% disapprove. The socioeconomic decomposition shows the incumbent support base is heavily concentrated among lower-income earners (≤2 minimum wage), Northeast residents, and retirees, while formal workers and middle/upper-income brackets show net negative approval, limiting the incumbent's ceiling.

### 3. Opposition Consolidation _(lowers)_

The opposition field has centered around distinct poles: Flávio Bolsonaro (PL, ~33% first round) leads as the primary challenger, followed by Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) and Romeu Zema (Novo), who aggregate secondary support from centrist and liberal-market voters. The withdrawal of other traditional centre-right figures like Aécio Neves simplifies the opposition landscape, potentially concentrating conservative and centre-right votes more effectively in a second-round runoff.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Since the 1997 constitutional amendment allowing consecutive terms, there have been four instances where an incumbent run for immediate reelection: 1998 (FHC, won), 2006 (Lula, won), 2014 (Dilma, won), and 2022 (Bolsonaro, lost). The incumbent success rate is 3 out of 4 (75%) for those who actually ran, though the 2022 failure marks the only time a sitting president lost under this current regime. Two other modern elections (2002, 2010) featured an incumbent barred by term limits, where the governing party maintained the presidency via a successional candidate.

## Bottom Line

The primary outcome uncertainty hinges on whether the polling gap in the second round remains within the margin of error or expands under current macro conditions. The market hinges on the official TSE totalization of results; current polling shows deep structural polarization that persists despite record-low unemployment and controlled inflation, suggesting the outcome will be decided by the relative turnout and consolidation of the fragmented opposition around a single runoff candidate.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to the political party of the candidate inaugurated as President of the United States on January 20, 2029. The resolution source is the consensus of the Associated Press, Fox News, and NBC. The market resolves once all three sources call the race for the same party. If all three sources have not called the race for the same party by inauguration day, the market resolves based on the actual inauguration. No intermediate metric exists for current resolution, as the event is binary and terminal.

## Source History & Current Reading

As of July 28, 2026, the political landscape is characterized by an incumbent Republican administration managing a 36% approval rating and a 4.2% unemployment rate. Democrats are navigating an open primary field, with recent polling from the University of New Hampshire (July 22, 2026) showing Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez leading with 22%, followed by Pete Buttigieg at 21%. The DNC has designated South Carolina as the opening contest for the 2028 primary calendar (July 25, 2026). Republican leadership is consolidating behind JD Vance as the preferred successor, while the GOP strategy for the 2026 midterms focuses on the 2025 tax-and-spending law rather than the currently unpopular Iran military conflict.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-26**: CBS News polling shows Trump overall job approval at 36% approve / 64% disapprove; Republican Senate/House candidates begin distancing strategies from Trump on foreign policy.
- **2026-07-25**: The Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee selects South Carolina to lead the 2028 presidential nominating calendar.
- **2026-07-23**: Fox News reporting details the New Hampshire poll where Ocasio-Cortez leads the Democratic primary field with 22% support.
- **2026-07-22**: University of New Hampshire Granite State Poll release: Ocasio-Cortez (22%) leads Buttigieg (21%) and Kelly (9%).
- **2026-07-21**: Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-LA) publicly breaks with Trump, calling for an end to Iran military action.

## Key Factors

### 1. Macroeconomic Fundamentals _(raises)_

The US economy is currently performing with an unemployment rate of 4.2%, which is near the natural rate, and projected real GDP growth of 2.2% for 2026. Historically, incumbents benefit when inflation is contained—here near the 2% Fed target—and unemployment is low. While the current Republican administration faces low approval, these economic indicators do not signal a recessionary environment, which typically drives incumbent loss. This stability removes a major drag on the governing party's narrative, potentially offsetting Trump’s lower approval numbers.

### 2. Battleground State Arithmetic _(uncertain)_

The electoral path to 270 relies on seven core battlegrounds (AZ, GA, MI, NV, NC, PA, WI) totaling 93 electoral votes. To reach the 270 threshold from a base of approximately 225 electoral votes (based on 2024 safe/likely mappings), a Democrat must capture at least 45 electoral votes from this 93-EV pool. In 2024, all seven states were within a +/- 2.1 percentage point margin. Democrats need a net improvement of 2-4 percentage points in vote share in these states to securely flip the results, making the outcome highly sensitive to narrow margin shifts.

### 3. Republican Succession and Party Mobilization _(lowers)_

President Trump is signaling JD Vance as his preferred 2028 successor, with Marco Rubio opting not to challenge him. Vance currently holds a commanding lead in early GOP primary polling and is executing a strategy to expand his appeal via a national book tour and diverse media appearances. Republican strategists are also concentrating on a $400 million war chest and a messaging strategy focused on domestic benefits (child tax credits, SALT caps) to insulate the party from the liabilities of the Iran conflict. A consolidated GOP brand under a more disciplined candidate like Vance could reduce the volatility seen in 2024.

### 4. Democratic Primary Processes _(uncertain)_

The DNC's selection of South Carolina to lead the 2028 calendar continues the party's shift toward racially diverse primary electorates, moving away from the old Iowa-New Hampshire model. While this affects coalition building and donor momentum, it creates uncertainty regarding which candidate profile will emerge as the national standard-bearer. Current polling shows a tight race between progressives like Ocasio-Cortez and moderates like Buttigieg. The party's ability to unify behind a candidate who can navigate the post-2024 political climate remains a critical variable.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

In the 13 presidential elections from 1976 through 2024, the incumbent party won 5 times and lost 8 times (38.5% win rate). In the subset of open-seat elections (where the incumbent president was not on the ballot), the incumbent party has won only 1 of the last 5 contests (1988, 2000, 2008, 2016, 2024), representing a 20% win rate for party handoffs. Studies from the American Presidency Project suggest parties holding the presidency for two or more consecutive terms (attempting a 'three-peat') face significant headwinds, averaging around 49% of the two-party vote share.

## Bottom Line

The outcome hinges on whether the Democratic nominee can overcome the 20% base-rate win frequency for incumbent-party successors by flipping the razor-thin margins (all within 2.1 percentage points in 2024) across the seven principal battleground states. Democratic chances will be fundamentally moved by the party's ability to unify its primary base and the degree to which the GOP nominee, likely JD Vance, can successfully detach the Republican brand from current foreign-policy liabilities (the Iran conflict) and Trump’s low national approval ratings.

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves based on the official final results reported by the Central Election Commission (CEC) of the Russian Federation. The core metric is the net change in parliamentary seat count for each party relative to the pre-September 2026 election baseline (United Russia: 324 seats, CPRF: 57, A Just Russia - For Truth: 27, LDPR: 21, New People: 13, Civil Platform: 1, Rodina: 1, Party of Growth: 1, Independents: 5). The successful party is the one with the largest positive delta in seats gained. If results are not definitively known by September 30, 2027, 11:59 PM ET, the market resolves to Other. As of July 28, 2026, the election has not occurred, meaning all parties are at a baseline of 0 net seat change.

## Source History & Current Reading

The authoritative pre-election seat distribution is derived from the September 2021 CEC allocation: United Russia 324, CPRF 57, A Just Russia 27, LDPR 21, New People 13, with single seats for Rodina, Civil Platform, and Party of Growth, and 5 Independents. Latest national polling (FOM, July 12, 2026) places United Russia at 49.3% vote share with a projected seat projection of 242. WCIOM (July 5, 2026) projects United Russia at 43.2% vote share with a projected 216 seats. Recent FOM approval ratings (July 24, 2026) show United Russia at 33%, a notable decrease from earlier 2026 peaks.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-24**: FOM and VTsIOM report United Russia approval ratings at 32.7-33%, the lowest since February 2022 due to war fatigue, inflation, and fuel shortages.
- **2026-07-23**: Meduza reports the Presidential Administration reduced United Russia's national electoral KPI target from 55-60% to 45-50%.
- **2026-07-12**: FOM national poll shows United Russia at 49.3% vote intention, with a parliamentary projection of 242 seats.
- **2026-07-05**: WCIOM poll shows United Russia at 43.2% vote intention, with a parliamentary projection of 216 seats.
- **2026-06-28**: FOM report shows United Russia at 52.1% vote intention.

## Key Factors

### 1. Institutional Ballot Access and Control _(lowers)_

The Central Election Commission has restricted access, confirming only 11 parties will appear on the federal ballot. The mixed electoral system of 225 party-list seats and 225 single-member districts (SMDs) is designed to favor the ruling party's administrative machinery. The reduction of 'cleared' SMD quotas for systemic opposition parties to between 10-13 seats (down from ~20 in 2021) limits potential gains for rivals to United Russia, reinforcing a managed political space.

### 2. Economic Strain and Kremlin KPI Calibration _(uncertain)_

Rising war fatigue, inflation, and fuel shortages have depressed United Russia's polling support to ~33%. In response, the Kremlin has lowered electoral KPIs to 45-50% nationwide, aiming for a more realistic appearance of legitimacy. While this suggests the Kremlin may permit slightly more visible opposition performance to prevent total alienation, the targets are rigorously calibrated to ensure United Russia maintains its constitutional majority regardless of the specific seat delta.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

In the 2011 election, United Russia lost 77 seats (315 to 238), while the Communist Party gained 45 (47 to 92). In 2016, United Russia gained 105 seats (238 to 343). In 2021, United Russia lost 19 seats (343 to 324), and the Communist Party gained 15 (42 to 57). The volatility in seat counts manifests every 5 years with large discrete jumps (net changes >20 seats) driven heavily by performance in single-member districts.

## Bottom Line

The primary uncertainty is whether the Kremlin's focus on a 'politically correct' result (45-50% KPI) will manifest as an intentional concession of SMD seats to systemic opposition or if the governing apparatus will override such concerns to maintain maximum control. Because the resolution depends on the 'greatest number of seats gained' (net change), a scenario where United Russia loses 10-20 seats while the opposition fails to gain any significant net ground leaves the 'most seats gained' outcome ambiguous. Watch for late-breaking announcements regarding local Kremlin district-level targeting, which remains the deciding mechanism for SMD seat distribution.
